strengths: Well-motivated design that meaningfully extends prior tool-graph and trajectory-memory approaches by attaching compact state summaries to graph edges, addressing a real gap (partial observability and progressively-clarified intent in multi-turn tool use) rather than simply combining existing components arbitrarily.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span four benchmarks (τ-bench, τ2-bench, ToolSandbox, ACEBench) and three base models (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o), plus an additional evaluation with GPT-5.1 and an online graph-construction setting without a training set.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the graph structure, the weight design (accuracy vs. efficiency terms), and the adaptive graph-leveraging mechanism (vs. GNN4Plan and a non-adaptive variant), which helps substantiate that each proposed component contributes to performance.

Training-free design is practically appealing, avoiding the substantial data-collection or RL costs required by SFT/RL baselines discussed in related work, while still improving over both memory-based and graph-based baselines.

The use of an invocable, on-demand summarization tool (rather than fixed-interval summarization) is a sensible mechanism for controlling recall cost and is empirically shown to help even without the graph (Table 4, row (i)).
weaknesses: No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-run statistics are reported for any experiment; several reported gains are very large (e.g., +32.8% to +43.0% on τ2-bench) which is unusual for a training-free retrieval-style augmentation and raises questions about run-to-run stability and statistical significance that are not addressed.

Key reproducibility details are missing or underspecified: how many rollouts were used to build training-set trajectories, sampling temperature/decoding settings, the value and sensitivity of the hyperparameter c in the weight formula, the top-k used for candidate suggestion, similarity thresholds for state matching, and embedding model used for state-summary similarity.
The ToolNet baseline is a reimplementation (original code not released), which weakens confidence that the comparison is fair and could partly explain the large performance gap versus SIT-Graph.

In the online/no-training-set setting (Section 5.3), the graph is built from test-time trajectories judged successful by an LLM-as-judge and then reused to evaluate subsequent test tasks; the paper does not discuss potential leakage, task ordering effects, or how much of the observed gain depends on the order in which test tasks are processed.

No analysis of the agent's own decision quality on whether to invoke the summarization/recall step (i.e., precision/recall of the episodic-vs-procedural switching decision itself), despite this being central to the paper's core claim of "human-like balance" between memory types.

No discussion of computational overhead/latency/token cost of building and querying the graph (embedding computation, storage growth with more trajectories, edge explosion as the tool set or trajectory count grows), which is relevant to the paper's own claim of "efficiency."
Presentation issues suggest incomplete polishing (e.g., Section 1 is titled "INSTRUCTION" instead of "Introduction"), and some figures/tables are dense and could be better organized for clarity.

The comparison set of baselines, while including memory- and graph-based methods, is relatively narrow (only 3 baselines); no comparison to a strong full-context/no-retrieval upper bound or other recent stateful-agent memory frameworks (e.g., Mem0, A-Mem, ArigGraph mentioned in related work) is provided in the main results, despite being discussed as related work.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated unification of episodic (state summary) and procedural (tool dependency) memory into a single graph structure, addressing a real gap between trajectory-level memory methods and pure tool-dependency graphs in multi-turn tool-use settings.

The method is training-free, relying only on accumulated rollouts/trajectories, making it practical to deploy without additional fine-tuning cost, and the paper also demonstrates an online variant that builds the graph from test-time trajectories when no training set is available (Section 5.3).

Extensive empirical evaluation spans four benchmarks (τ-bench, τ2-bench, ToolSandbox, ACEBench) and three base models (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o), with SIT-Graph consistently outperforming ReasoningBank, ToolNet, and naive retrieval baselines, often by large margins (e.g., +32.8%/+43.0% on τ2-bench).

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contributions of the graph structure, edge weights, state information, the efficiency term in the weight formula, and the adaptive (vs. non-adaptive / GNN4Plan) traversal strategy, providing reasonable evidence that each component matters.

The comparison showing GPT-4.1 + SIT-Graph surpassing GPT-5.1 on several benchmarks is a compelling demonstration of practical value of experience reuse relative to simply using a stronger base model.
The paper is clearly written with helpful illustrative figures (Fig. 1-3) that make the construction and inference procedures easy to follow.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines two known ideas (episodic-style state summaries and tool-dependency graphs) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the primary contribution is the integration and adaptive routing policy, which, while reasonable, is not deeply novel.

The ToolNet baseline is a self-reimplementation (footnote 1) since the original is not open-sourced, which raises fairness/reproducibility concerns, as differences in implementation details could unduly favor SIT-Graph.

Key implementation details are missing or underspecified: how the agent decides whether to invoke the summarization tool (the criterion/threshold governing this binary decision is not described), what embedding/similarity model is used for state comparison, and how the constant c in Eq. 1 is chosen/tuned (no sensitivity analysis).

No variance/standard deviation or multiple-run statistics are reported despite LLM-based agents being stochastic; single-run point estimates make it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains, especially where baseline improvements are sometimes marginal or negative.

Scalability of the graph is not discussed: as more trajectories accumulate, edges may store multiple overlapping state summaries and nodes/edges could grow substantially; there is no analysis of memory footprint, retrieval latency, or how the graph is pruned/maintained over time.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section discussing failure modes (e.g., cases where state summaries are inaccurate or where multiple domains produce conflicting successful trajectories for the same tool pair), which would strengthen scientific honesty and reproducibility.

Evaluation is restricted to English, simulated user-agent benchmarks; no analysis of real deployment costs (e.g., added latency per turn from state summarization and similarity comparison) is provided, which is relevant to practical significance.
